One-sentence judgment: business analytics is not exporting the data and making a chart, but turning a vague business problem into a recalculable metric definition, a handover-ready report, and a reviewable statement of the basis. O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed, SVP 7.0 to below 8.0) and marks Bright Outlook, with interest code CIE. The core boundary is: you can define metrics and granularity, write and review queries, do quality checks, build models and visualizations, and explain limitations to decision makers; but you cannot go beyond data access rights and compliance requirements, you cannot approve the basis on behalf of the business owner, and you cannot release unverified output externally or use it as a commitment.

Signals for continued exploration: you ask how a metric is calculated rather than only looking at the chart; you can rewrite a vague business problem as a verifiable definition; you are willing to recheck data lineage, basis, and access rights; you can state the strength of evidence when uncertain and explain limitations to non-technical decision makers; and you accept a daily work style dominated by desktop analysis, report maintenance, and cross-departmental communication.

Conditions for pausing high-cost investment first: you have not yet completed a full closed loop from clarifying the decision question, confirming the basis and granularity, retrieving data and checking quality, modeling and visualizing, to business-side review; or you only want to make charts, are unwilling to check the basis and data sources, and are unwilling to review queries section by section when challenged; and do not treat being able to use a certain BI tool as proof that you can independently deliver recalculable metrics.

Education, qualifications, and authorization must be checked separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed, SVP 7.0 to below 8.0), and most positions require a four-year bachelor's degree while some do not; education and certificates are usually employer preferences rather than a unified license, and this occupation has no unified practice license; data access and release rights are determined by the organization's data classification, row and column level permissions, and applicable compliance requirements; for the current wage figures of the United States and China, the evidence route for this item is that there is no data that can be safely used, so this page does not fix static values and provides only official query entry points and boundary notes.

In one sentence: this is a role that turns business problems into recalculable metrics and reviewable recommendations, and its outputs are recalculable metrics, dashboards, anomaly analysis, basis statements, and recommendations for decision makers; it is not the owner of the business basis and does not replace data engineering, data science, or data governance duties. Current wage figures for the United States and China are not fixed on this page: for the United States the evidence route provides an official query entry point for the exact occupation code, and for mainland China the gap, sources, and occupation mapping boundaries are retained.

Editorial task summary: the work of this occupation falls into three categories: first, questions and basis (clarifying the decision question, confirming metric definitions and granularity, specifying the denominator and time window, and agreeing the basis owner and approval process); second, data retrieval and delivery (writing and reviewing queries, doing quality checks and explaining anomalies, modeling and visualizing, writing report and dashboard specifications, and maintaining reusable templates and documents); third, review and operation (reviewing conclusions with business counterparts, explaining assumptions and limitations, releasing and monitoring metric changes, and providing technical support and metadata updates to users). All three share the same chain centered on recalculation and review.
Questions and basis

Clarify the decision question → confirm the metric definition and granularity → specify the denominator and time window → agree the basis owner and approval process → record assumptions and data sources → form a reviewable basis statement.
Data retrieval and delivery

Write and review queries → do quality checks and explain anomalies → build the metric and dimension model → design and produce visualizations → write report and dashboard specifications → maintain templates and documents and hand over.

Review conclusions with business counterparts → explain assumptions and the strength of evidence → release metrics and dashboards according to permissions → monitor metric changes and refresh timeliness → provide support to users and update metadata → iterate the basis and products based on feedback.

Editorial adjacent task comparison: BI focuses on business-facing intelligence, reporting, and tool maintenance; data science, data supply, databases, operations research, management diagnosis, and market research have different objects and methods and may also carry ongoing reporting or cross-cutting duties. Position titles do not define the basis ownership, data permissions, or exclusive outputs of every organization.
Core purpose

Let decision makers see the current business state under a clear basis and strength of evidence: support operations and decisions with recalculable metrics, explainable anomalies, and traceable basis statements, and keep metrics consistent across the organization.
Main objects and basis

The objects are the business question and decision timing, detail and summary tables in the data warehouse, metric and dimension definitions, report and dashboard products, and data permissions and compliance requirements; the basis is the metric contract and basis documentation, data lineage and quality rules, the organization's data classification and access control requirements, applicable privacy and industry compliance requirements, and the business owner's approval of the basis.
Core process
Clarify the decision question, confirm the basis and granularity, retrieve data and check quality, model and visualize, review with business counterparts, and release and monitor metric changes.
Main outputs

Recalculable metrics and a metric dictionary, reports and dashboards, anomaly and attribution analysis, basis and assumption statements, one-page recommendations for decision makers, query and transformation scripts, quality check and test records, and a reusable template and document library.
Responsible parties

Editorial role check example: assign clear responsibility for metric definitions, queries, charts, and data quality, and check with the target organization who is actually responsible for business basis approval, platform maintenance, permission control, and external disclosure; this page does not specify that every organization must have the same team or role.
Authority and approval

Editorial permission check suggestion: check actual permissions, approvals, and data rules before accessing data domains, releasing metrics, and providing materials externally; row and column level control is an optional implementation example and is not a unified legal requirement for every unit in this occupation. Technical proficiency does not automatically grant authorization.
Conclusion boundaries

Metrics and dashboards state what the business looks like under the given basis and data quality conditions; they do not equal causal conclusions and do not replace business judgment and authorized decisions, and they are updated as the basis is revised, data is refreshed, and the business changes; the version and refresh time should be stated when citing them.

Before starting, check at least six items: the position duties (leaning toward metric engineering, report delivery, or business analysis), the data domain and permission scope, the basis approval process and who the business owner is, the technology and tool stack (SQL and BI platforms), the delivery cadence and duty/support requirements, and whether it carries data compliance and privacy related responsibility.
Occupation basis

O*NET-SOC15-2051.01 Business Intelligence Analysts, belonging to the SOC15-2051 Data Scientists parent group (mathematical science occupations), not the Computer and Information Analysts group. The detailed occupation has JobZoneFour, BrightOutlook, and CIE. O*NET2025 industry data come from the Data Scientists parent group: professional, scientific, and technical services 25%, finance and insurance 19%, information 12%, enterprise management 10%, other 34% (including administrative support and health care and social assistance). These are not the BI detailed occupation's industry composition and not industry wages. The mainland China occupation classification and US 15-2051.01 must be checked against actual duties; the one-to-one mapping to a detailed category in the 2022 compendium was not completed this round, and a publication entry point is not taken as proof that no detailed category exists or that no license is needed.
Education and training paths

O*NET new entrant education Q&A for the detailed occupation: 68% bachelor's, 23% master's, 5% associate's or other two-year degree; this is not the education composition of incumbents. JobZoneFour/SVP7 to below 8 is a summary of the preparation level; most require an undergraduate degree but some do not, usually involving several years of preparation; check the target position's education and experience separately, and the BLS parent group's typical bachelor's degree, experience None, and OJT None cannot replace the detailed occupation's requirements. This round did not check whether any jurisdiction has a specific individual license or industry condition; education, tool certification, and organizational data permissions are checked separately, and neither O*NET nor an occupation classification notice can prove that no practice license exists in China.

The O*NET detailed profile has 51 software categories; US 2025 hiring hot technology has 100 specific skills and 14 InDemand. SQL35%, PowerBI20%, Python20%, Tableau19%, SAP19%, Excel17%, R10%, AWS9%; these are hiring mentions rather than an adoption rate or occupational replacement. Metric contracts, models, lineage, and check methods are editorial work examples.

Data permissions, connections and basis, and refresh are editorial risk scenarios; permission control, quality alerts, and review are arranged according to actual system rules, and row and column level filtering is not a unified legal requirement for every position.

This round did not check whether any jurisdiction has a specific individual license or industry condition; education, tool certification, and organizational data permissions are checked separately, and neither O*NET nor an occupation classification notice can prove that no practice license exists in China. Actual data processing is checked against applicable requirements and organizational authorization, and policy catalogues and occupation classification notices are only discovery entry points.

O*NET detailed occupation context: 91% regular work hours, 67% 40h per week, 33% more than 40h; this is not a fixed arrangement for every position. Business intelligence analysts (O*NET-SOC 15-2051.01, Business Intelligence Analysts) produce financial and market intelligence by querying data repositories and generating periodic reports, and design methods to identify data patterns and trends from available information sources. Daily work includes: producing standard or custom reports for executives, managers, clients, and other stakeholders; maintaining or updating business intelligence tools, databases, dashboards, systems, or methods; managing the timely flow of business intelligence information to users; providing technical support for existing reports, dashboards, or other tools; identifying and analyzing industry or geographic trends with business strategy implications; writing specifications for reports, dashboards, or other output; creating business intelligence tools or systems (including the design of related databases, spreadsheets, or output); collecting business intelligence data from industry reports, public information, field reports, or paid sources; disseminating information about updates to tools, reports, or metadata; conducting or coordinating tests to ensure intelligence matches defined requirements; synthesizing current business intelligence or trend data to support recommendations for action; analyzing competitive market strategies by analyzing related product, market, or share trends; using business intelligence tools to identify or monitor existing and potential customers; communicating with clients, competitors, suppliers, professional organizations, and others to stay informed about industry trends; maintaining a library of model documents, templates, or other reusable knowledge assets; creating or reviewing technical design documents to ensure accurate development of reporting solutions; and analyzing technology trends to identify markets for future product development or to improve sales of existing products. It carries responsibility for metric quality, basis statements, and the strength of evidence behind recommendations, but does not replace the business basis owner, data platform teams, or data governance duties.

The 17 official tasks are all Core, with 41 general activities, 12 detailed activities, and 57 context items; the tasks cover reporting, BI tool maintenance, information dissemination, technical support, market trends, output specifications, tool design, data collection, testing, recommendations, and document templates. JobZoneFour and BrightOutlook describe the detailed occupation and are not every position's full duties.

paragraphs: This page compares business intelligence analysts with five adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: occupational direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which direction each preference suits better. Adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupational descriptions, and this does not mean position titles are interchangeable.

Evidence note: occupational directions and core outputs are based on the official descriptions of O*NET 15-2051.01 and the adjacent entries (US basis); basis ownership, data permissions, and qualification requirements must be verified separately for each organization and jurisdiction, and this page does not present any direction as a shortcut to a career change.

The table below compares business intelligence analysts with adjacent directions in duties and outputs; the judgment is based on main outputs, responsibility objects, and required permissions, not on how similar the position titles are.

Data scientists develop predictive models and inference methods and are more exploratory; this occupation emphasizes stable metrics, ongoing reporting, and a recalculable basis, with outputs aimed at daily decisions rather than one-off modeling.
If you would rather do modeling and algorithm exploration, look first at the data scientist direction; if you would rather make metrics solid and the basis clear, look first at this occupation.
Derive predictions and inferences from data using statistics and machine learning, with outputs mainly models, experimental conclusions, and exploratory analysis.
Data analysts and data scientists (Data Scientists)

Data engineers are the supply side of data products and are responsible for pipelines, storage, and operational reliability; this occupation is the consuming and verifying side and is responsible for metric definitions, quality checks, and decision-facing presentation.

If you would rather do platform and pipeline engineering, look first at the data engineer direction; if you would rather define metrics for the business and explain results, look first at this occupation.
Build and maintain data pipelines, storage, and platforms, with outputs mainly reliable data supply and pipelines.
Data engineers (Data Engineers)

Management analysts make recommendations at the organization and process level and do not carry metric engineering or data product maintenance; this occupation centers on recalculable data products and basis consistency, and conclusions must match the strength of the data evidence.
If you would rather do organizational diagnosis and process improvement, look first at management analysts; if you would rather do data products and metric governance, look first at this occupation.
Diagnose organizational and process problems and propose improvements, with outputs mainly diagnostic reports and reform recommendations.
Management analysts (Management Analysts)

Market research analysts focus on research design and market judgment, and marketing specialists focus on campaign and acquisition execution; this occupation focuses on internal metric consistency and report products and does not carry marketing campaign responsibility.
If you would rather do market research and marketing planning, look first at the market research direction; if you would rather do metrics and report products, look first at this occupation.
Design and run market research and assess market and customer needs, with outputs mainly research conclusions and marketing recommendations.
Market research analysts and marketing specialists (Market Research Analysts and Marketing Specialists)

Search marketing strategists are responsible for marketing channel performance, and analysis serves campaign decisions; this occupation serves the organization's overall metrics and decisions and does not carry the business responsibility of channel campaigns.

If you would rather do channel campaigns and performance optimization, look first at search marketing strategists; if you would rather do cross-domain metrics and decision support, look first at this occupation.
Plan search and performance marketing strategies and optimize campaigns, with outputs mainly acquisition performance and campaign analysis.
Search marketing strategists (Search Marketing Strategists)

Computer and information systems managers own platforms and delivery resources and are responsible for systems; this occupation defines metrics, produces reports, and explains anomalies within the given platform and permissions and does not carry system building or team management duties.

If you would rather be responsible for systems and teams, look first at computer and information systems managers; if you would rather go deep into metrics and business interpretation, look first at this occupation.
Plan and manage information systems and team delivery, with outputs mainly system capability, project delivery, and technology roadmaps.
Computer and information systems managers (Computer and Information Systems Managers)

Conclusion: the choice of direction is based on main outputs, responsibility objects, and required permissions, not on how similar the names are; once a direction is chosen, check item by item the target position's duty boundaries, data domain and permission scope, basis approval process, and tool stack, and keep written confirmation.

paragraphs: Students or career changers preparing to enter this occupation

First complete one full closed loop with fictional data: rewrite a business problem as a metric definition and granularity, write a recalculable query, do quality checks and explain anomalies, produce a non-misleading visualization, and explain limitations to a non-technical reader; then check the target position's duty boundaries (leaning toward metric engineering, report delivery, or business analysis) and its data permission scope.
Practicing business intelligence analysts

Editorial collaboration suggestion: use tools for reviewable steps such as SQL drafts, chart suggestions, and natural language querying and summarization; query correctness, basis consistency, sampling and denominators, permission compliance, and release conclusions must still be checked section by section by the analyst and documented. Specific division of work and processes are checked against the target organization.
Data platform and governance teams

Editorial collaboration suggestion: before introducing natural language querying or automatic query generation, first clarify the usable data domains, permissions and row and column level control, who is responsible for reviewing generated results, and how audit trails are kept, so that any output can be traced back to the original tables and the metric contract, and the business owner keeps the right to approve the basis. Specific division of work and processes are checked against the target organization.
Education and development

Focus training on metric definition, SQL and data models, quality checks and lineage tracing, visualization and dissemination, and explaining limitations to decision makers; at the same time train the habit of checking tool output, especially denominators, time windows, join relationships, and sampling bias.

paragraphs: Boundary: this section describes occupational risk and responsibility boundaries, not an evaluation of any individual or organization; specific procedures and handling processes are determined by the applicable jurisdiction, organizational data governance rules, and work authorization.

Task-related risk scenarios include basis drift, failure of permission filtering, wrong generated queries, expired refreshes, missing lineage, and unauthorized disclosure. The controls below are editorial suggestions and actual duty rules are checked separately; there is no material on risk occurrence rates or intervention effects.

O*NET tasks and context support the work background; the specific metric, permission, refresh, and documentation risks are editorial scenarios. The ILO study examines task exposure only and does not prove this occupation's failure rates, compliance conclusions, or the effects of the measures below.
Analyst and business owner
Drift in denominators and time window bases makes conclusions in different departments conflict with each other, and it becomes hard to tell whether the problem is the basis or a business change.

Editorial check suggestion: maintain the metric contract and run regression tests; basis changes are approved by the business owner and documents and dashboard notes are updated in step. Implement according to actual rules and permissions; risk elimination is not guaranteed.
Adjusting the denominator or statistical scope without approval to suit the conclusion.
Analyst and data governance and security teams
Failure of permission filtering or overly broad shared links leads to sensitive data being displayed beyond authorization, with compliance and trust consequences.

Analyst (the individual)
When a query generated by a generative tool has a wrong join or a misunderstood basis, the numbers look reasonable but mean something wrong.

Publishing a tool-generated result directly without independent recalculation.

An unlabeled dashboard refresh delay makes decisions use stale data and reach wrong conclusions.

Editorial check suggestion: show the refresh time and set quality alerts; confirm data timeliness and completeness before key decisions. Implement according to actual rules and permissions; risk elimination is not guaranteed.

Keeping key logic in personal scripts without documentation or handover.

Providing or disclosing sensitive data or personal information without a compliance basis and documentation leads to serious consequences.

entries.answer: Produce periodic reports and business intelligence by querying data repositories: clarify the business question, confirm metric definitions and granularity, write and review queries, do quality checks and explain anomalies, build the metric and dimension model, design reports and dashboards, review conclusions with business counterparts and write a one-page recommendation, release and monitor metric changes according to permissions, and maintain the template and document library, update metadata, and provide technical support to users.
entries.question: What do business intelligence analysts do every day?

entries.answer: The main risks are basis and denominator drift causing conflicting departmental conclusions, failure of permission filtering causing display beyond authorization, wrong joins in queries generated by generative tools making numbers look reasonable, unlabeled dashboard delays causing decisions to use stale data, missing basis and lineage documents making conclusions impossible to recalculate, and the compliance risk of providing sensitive data externally; controls rely on the metric contract and regression tests, least privilege and row and column level control, section-by-section review against samples, refresh timeliness labeling and quality alerts, and a clear release and escalation process.

entries.answer: Fit signals are being able to ask how a metric is calculated, rewriting a vague business problem as a verifiable definition, being willing to recheck data lineage and permissions, and being able to explain limitations to non-technical decision makers; being able to use a certain BI tool is not enough to prove competence, and what matters is whether there is reviewable metric delivery and basis documentation.
